TITLE: Why big business fears 'Raynernomics' — and Andy Burnham
PUBLISHED: 2026-05-16T12:25Z (The Sunday Times)
AUTHOR: David Smith, Economics Editor

"Raynernomics" — the approach that former deputy prime minister Angela Rayner would take if she were to win a Labour leadership contest — is all too easy to define, and financial markets and businesses are already adopting the brace position in case it becomes a reality.

"In the absence of any detail from Andy Burnham, who, should he win the Makerfield by-election, will be a leadership candidate, possibly the favourite, it is reasonable to assume that his economics would be similar to Rayner's, which is why there was a sell-off for UK government bonds (gilts) and the pound on Friday."

For the past two years, business people have regarded the Starmer-Reeves approach of higher taxes, higher minimum wages and increased intervention as about as bad as it could get. They may be about to discover that clinging on to nurse might have been better than something worse.

RAYNER POSITIONS (from CWU conference speech in Bournemouth this week):
- Labour must "be the party of working people"
- "Living standards are barely higher than they were a decade and a half ago"
- "People feel hopeless — that the cost of living crisis will never end — and now they see oil and gas companies use global instability to post record profits"
- "Once again, ordinary people are paying the price for decisions they didn't make. It's no wonder that across the UK, working people feel the system is rigged against them."
- Aggressively redistributionist: "an economy that does not work for the majority, with wealth concentrated in too few hands"
- Attacked "decisions like cutting winter fuel allowance" — Reeves's first big announcement in July 2024
- Unlike Reeves, Rayner has NOT ruled out a wealth tax
- Leaked memo last year advocated higher taxes on dividends and banks, bringing more higher-paid people into the additional-rate 45% net
- Employment Rights Act "just the first step" — fair pay agreement in social care, rising minimum wage, building boom, renters' reform, ending leasehold "feudal" system

POTENTIAL CHANCELLOR: Ed Miliband described as candidate to succeed Reeves under a Rayner premiership — flagship 2015 policy: annual mansion tax on high-value properties.

BURNHAM CHARACTERISATION: Greater Manchester mayor, regarded as significantly to the left of Starmer and "more genuinely Labour" than either he or Wes Streeting.
